The freshwater pearl mussel Margaritifera margaritifera begins its life cycle with an extraordinarily small neonate, the prodissoconch shell measuring just 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] at the moment of birth. This minuscule initial dimension is typical of unionoid bivalves, which release fully formed glochidia larvae rather than free-swimming veligers. After a brief post-eclosion period, these parasitic larvae must attach to the gills of a suitable salmonid host to complete their development. The specific timing of the hatching event has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions: when maintained at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the age at birth is approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], a relatively rapid developmental pace that reflects the energetic constraints of the yolk-dependent, non-feeding larval stage. Following successful attachment to the host fish, the glochidia undergo a period of encystment and metamorphosis before excysting as recently metamorphosed juveniles. The shell length at the moment of settlement onto the riverbed substratum has been recorded at 0.03 centimeters , representing an almost imperceptible size increase from the birth dimension, yet marking a critical ecological transition from parasitism to independent benthic life.

Upon excystment from the fish host, the post-metamorphic juveniles bury themselves within the interstitial spaces of the gravel substrate, where they initiate a prolonged growth phase that spans several decades. The ultimate shell length attained by fully grown adults of Margaritifera margaritifera has been documented from extensive field surveys, with the largest individuals reaching 17.6 centimeters [Li = 17.6 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger members of the Margaritiferidae family. This final dimension is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 196 grams [Wwi = 196 grams], a value estimated from allometric scaling relationships for unionoid bivalves when body size is taken into account. Such an asymptotic size is achieved only after many years of continuous somatic investment, as the mussel slowly accumulates shell material and soft tissue mass. The growth trajectory of this species is notably decelerated compared to other freshwater bivalves, reflecting the oligotrophic, nutrient-poor streams it typically inhabits. Sedentary and long-lived, these mussels allocate resources predominantly to shell thickening and tissue maintenance throughout most of their adult lives, with measurable annual growth increments becoming vanishingly small in older age classes.

The attainment of sexual maturity in Margaritifera margaritifera occurs remarkably late in life relative to most freshwater bivalves, a life-history trait that renders populations highly vulnerable to disturbance. Field studies employing size-at-age reconstructions from shell annuli have established that the shell length at puberty is 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to an age of approximately 20 years. This delayed pubertal development reflects the slow metabolic pace and cold-water environment typical of the species' habitats, where low food availability and extended winters constrain growth rates. Sub-adults below this shell length show no evidence of gonadal activity, whereas individuals exceeding 6 centimeters consistently exhibit developing gametes during the reproductive season. The onset of gametogenesis thus occurs only after the mussel has accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of reproductive effort. This protracted pre-reproductive period is an extreme example of the K-selected life-history strategy observed in many freshwater bivalves, prioritising individual survival and iterative reproduction over early breeding.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial but concentrated within a remarkably brief annual spawning window. When water temperatures reach 17 °C [T = 17 °C], females release glochidia at a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 22,000 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 22,000 larvae per day], as inferred from direct counts of larval release in captive broodstock. This daily fecundity represents the product of a single, tightly synchronised annual spawning event, with each gravid female discharging her entire larval brood over a period of several days. The temperature dependence of this process is critical: larval development within the marsupial gills proceeds only above a thermal threshold, and the synchronous mass release at 17 °C likely serves to saturate host fish during their upstream migration. Such a high instantaneous reproductive rate partially compensates for the extraordinary mortality suffered during the parasitic larval stage, where fewer than one in a million glochidia successfully metamorphose and settle. The entire reproductive strategy is thus geared toward maximising encounter probability with the specific salmonid host, rather than toward per-offspring investment.

Longevity data for Margaritifera margaritifera place the species among the most extreme examples of extended lifespan in the animal kingdom. At a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the typical maximum lifespan observed in natural populations reaches approximately 280 years [am = approximately 280 years], a figure consistent with long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in undisturbed Scandinavian rivers. This extraordinary longevity is accompanied by negligible senescence in later life stages, as older individuals continue to filter-feed and reproduce with undiminished efficiency. The physiological mechanisms underpinning such extended survival are thought to involve exceptionally low basal metabolic rates, efficient antioxidant defences, and the protective properties of the thick nacreous shell against predation and physical abrasion. Comparatively, the life span of 280 years far exceeds that of any other European freshwater bivalve and is rivalled only by certain deep-sea and Antarctic molluscs. This remarkable durability, however, comes at the cost of extreme sensitivity to habitat degradation: because recruitment is sporadic and growth is slow, populations that lose their adult cohort through pollution or river engineering may require centuries to recover.
